description: We are a team of six university students studying Software Engineering, brought together by our shared passion for space, technology, and innovation. We aim to combine our software development skills, creativity, and teamwork to build meaningful solutions to real-world challenges using NASA’s open data and resources.
summary: GeoTwin is an interactive web platform that helps mission planners find the best Earth analog for permanent Moon and Mars bases. It maps 183 analog sites in 9 regions, including three in Türkiye, and scores each one against the Moon or Mars on six engineering criteria: topography, temperature, thermal behavior, geology, water/ice and habitability. A Mission Planner turns a chosen site, mission scenario (ISRU, rover, habitat or astrobiology) and duration into a phased test plan, and the ASTRA-AI advisor answers comparison questions in plain language. NASA POWER (MERRA-2/CERES) climate data is retrieved through its API for six stations and used for a climate-match check, while ASTER GDEM, MOLA/HiRISE, MODIS, ESA, SCAR and REMA serve as reference datasets. GeoTwin answers the challenge by identifying and ranking Earth locations that analog permanent lunar and Martian base environments. It matters because every hardware test on the Moon or Mars is extremely costly, so choosing the right Earth site early saves money, time and risk for agencies, universities and student teams.
details:
What it does
GeoTwin is a browser-based Planetary Analog Explorer. The user chooses a target body, Mars or the Moon, and sees 183 Earth analog sites in 9 world regions on an interactive map. Each site has a similarity percentage and a six-criteria profile: topography, temperature, thermal behavior, geology, water/ice and habitability. Users can search by site, country or crater, and a site panel shows how closely a place of interest matches the target. For example, the Karapınar sinkholes in Türkiye score 88.0% against lunar skylights, while Haughton Crater scores 97.6%.

How it works
The Mission Planner takes a site, a mission scenario (ISRU, rover mobility, habitat shielding or astrobiology) and a duration, and weights the criteria for that scenario (45%, 35% and 20% for the top three). It then outputs a phased engineering test plan for 14–30 days, 90–180 days or 500+ days. The ASTRA-AI advisor answers questions such as “which site is best for ice mining?”. For six stations, the site retrieves annual climate values from the NASA POWER API (MERRA-2/CERES): temperature, solar irradiance, precipitation and wind. It uses them for a climate-match check against each target body. ASTER GDEM V003, Mars MOLA/HiRISE, MODIS, ESA, SCAR and REMA are reference datasets for our criteria. The six-criteria scores are our team’s engineering assessment informed by these references.

Benefits and intended impact
Choosing an analog site is slow and manual today. GeoTwin gives space agencies, universities and student teams one comparable score per mission, so they can pick a test site faster and justify the choice. Because Moon and Mars hardware tests are extremely costly, choosing the right Earth site early reduces risk, money and field time.

Tools
HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single web page, with no installation or special hardware. Leaflet for maps, Esri World Imagery and CARTO for map layers, the NASA POWER API for climate data, and an optional Gemini model for ASTRA-AI.

Creativity
Most analog resources are static lists. GeoTwin gives separate Moon and Mars scores, adapts the ranking to the mission type, turns a site choice into a test plan, and lets users ask questions in plain language. It also adds Turkish analogs (Nemrut, Karapınar, Cappadocia) that existing catalogs rarely cover.

Factors we considered
We designed the criteria so that one site is not “best” for every mission, because a rover test and an ice-mining test need different terrain. We kept the data transparent by separating NASA-retrieved climate values from our own engineering scores. We also prioritized a clear interface that works in any browser. Current limitations are that NASA POWER data covers six stations and the criteria scores are not yet computed from raw datasets. Extending live NASA data to all 183 sites is our next step.
